parts.name: The white church
parts.stand: In the open space beside the church, where you can take in its whole shape.

paras.t: This soft, white, almost sculpted building is Panagia Paraportiani, the Church of Our Lady. Its odd, lovable shape, Wikipedia says, makes it one of the most photographed places in the world.
The whitewash can be dazzling in full sun. Sunglasses help, and the stone underfoot can be uneven, so look down now and then as you move along.
Wikivoyage goes further: of all the churches on Mykonos, it calls this the most impressive.

And there's a lot of competition. Mykonos is crowded with churches. The usual explanation is that for many years islanders had to build a church on their land before they could build a house. Wikivoyage calls this one the most photographed of them all.

parts.name: Five churches in one
parts.stand: Move along the outside as far as the path allows, looking up at the upper level.

paras.t: Here's the secret of that shape. It isn't one church, it's five, joined together. Four sit at ground level, and the fifth is built on top of them.

The four below are dedicated to Saint Eustathios, Saint Sozon, the Saints Anargyroi, and Saint Anastasia. They form the base, and the fifth church rests above them. As you move along, see if you can tell where one ends and the next begins.
It went up slowly. Construction began in 1425 and wasn't finished until the 17th century, around 200 years from start to finish.

parts.name: By the castle gate
parts.stand: Stand where you can see the lanes of the Kastro quarter around the church.

paras.t: This quarter is Kastro, the oldest part of town. The church's name, Paraportiani, means Our Lady of the Side Gate, because its entrance was at the side gate into the Kastro.

A gate into what? A medieval castle. Here's how it came about. After Constantinople fell in the Fourth Crusade in 1204, Mykonos passed to Andrea Ghisi. The castle was built here in 1207 by the Ghisi family, who controlled the island at the time.
The castle didn't last. It was destroyed in the 16th century, and when the town grew in the 18th century, new buildings covered what was left. The church outlived the walls it was named for.
Just a few steps away is the Folklore Museum, set in an 18th-century sea captain's house, if you'd like to see how island families once lived.
The first stones were laid here in 1425, and the last around two hundred years later. Whoever started it never saw the shape you're looking at now.
